## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
Nothing has run yet, and the starting architecture scored 0 on both seeds. In the code, actions are type*Y*X + y*X + x with DONE last, and the anchor is the top-left cell. For this world the observation has 27 channels and the grid is 8×8. The starting network (a per-column 1×1 stem, 3×3 context and a head that pools over each footprint) can already express the needed local checks: where a brick lands, whether every cell it fills is still missing, and what it seals. My guess is that it fails because of too few updates: 4 epochs leave 131k steps, about 32 updates of 4096. One epoch gives about 426k steps (104 updates). I also raise gamma and lambda so the end-of-episode bonus reaches earlier steps, and lower entropy to sharpen greedy evaluation. Candidate 1 isolates the recipe change. Candidate 2 adds a normalised residual network with the legal-action mask as input on the same recipe. Candidate 3 tests 2 epochs on that network.

### Round 2
All three round-1 trials scored exactly 0 on dev and 0 on training success. That covers the baseline net and a GroupNorm-residual net, with 1 or 2 PPO epochs and 240k–425k steps. The recipe changes did not move training success either, so sample count is probably not the bottleneck. The task warns that the world may differ from its description. A plausible failure that no recipe could fix is a spatial head that assumes the wrong layout: if the action index order (y/x order, the anchor corner, or footprint orientation) differs from the stated one, a fully convolutional head scores the wrong cells. No 3x3 receptive field can fix that, because the mapping is not local. This round therefore tests heads that can learn any action layout. The first combines a dense flattened-feature head with the convolutional head. The second is a pure MLP over the flattened observation and mask. The third is the combined head with a stronger exploration and credit-assignment recipe.

### Round 3
After six trials, every seed has scored 0 on both dev and training success. That covers 1 or 2 epochs, the conv and dense heads, a pure MLP, and an exploration-heavy recipe. Since even the layout-agnostic MLP scored 0, the action layout is probably not the cause. The likelier cause is that no tested network can easily work out where a brick lands and whether the target is filled at that height. All the 2D nets so far put the layers together as input channels in the first 1x1 layer, so they have to learn something like 'look up the target at the height given by the max column height under the footprint' with no structure to help.

So this round tests a layer-factored net. It runs the same learned 2D convolutions on every height layer, with learned mixing between adjacent layers. It scores each (type, layer, anchor) by pooling over the footprint, then takes a soft maximum over layers. All three candidates use this net and the 1-epoch recipe. They vary width (sample count) and update frequency.

### Round 4
All 9 trials scored exactly 0 on both training and dev success. That covers 2D conv nets, norm-residual nets, hybrid dense heads, a pure MLP that makes no layout assumption, per-layer nets, and recipes with 1, 2 or 4 epochs, different entropy, gamma and batch sizes. When every architecture fails the same way, a layout mismatch is unlikely; a shared learning failure is more likely. My best guess, which is inferred and not observed: random early placements mostly add extra cells, so continuing has a strongly negative value (about -1 over the 33-placement cap). Calling DONE gives 0, so its advantage (about +1) dwarfs that of a good placement (about +0.07). PPO probably collapses to calling DONE early, stops exploring placements, and greedy evaluation then fails. This round tests that guess three ways: slowing how fast the DONE logit learns (two strengths), and using high entropy with a shorter horizon on the unchanged network. The fixed start, the uncapped 0.2 scale and the untouched advantage sign leave some risk.
